reasoning.Student A:
My goal is to be matched to the best school possible according to my preferences: w > z > y > x.

I have the following priority ranks:
w: 1
x: 2
y: 1
z: 2

Since I have top priority at both w and y, I should rank the one I prefer higher. I prefer w, so I rank w first.

My second choice is z. I have priority rank 2 at z. If I get rejected from w, I will automatically be considered at z. Therefore, I should rank z second.

My third choice is y. I have priority rank 1 at y. If I get rejected from both w and z, I will automatically be considered at y. Therefore, I should rank y third.

My last choice is x. I have priority rank 2 at x. If I get rejected from w, z, and y, I will automatically be considered at x. Therefore, I should rank x last.

Therefore, my ranking should be w > z > y > x.
reasoning.Student B:
My goal is to be matched with the best school possible according to my preferences: z > y > w > x. I also know my priority rank at each school: w: 2, x: 1, y: 2, z: 1. Most applicants prefer y > x > w > z.

School z is my top choice and I have the highest priority (rank 1) there. This makes it very likely I will be matched to z if I apply.

School y is my second choice, and I have priority rank 2 there. Since most applicants prefer y, there will be competition for y. However, my lower priority rank makes it less likely I'll be matched to y if I apply.

School w is my third choice, and I have priority rank 2 there. Since most applicants seem to dislike z, w, and x, it is less competitive than y.

School x is my last choice, but I have the highest priority (rank 1) there. However, I would only want to go to x if I am rejected from all other schools.

Given that I will be automatically considered at all remaining schools on my list if I am rejected from a school, I should rank the schools in order of my preference. This is because if I am rejected from my top choice, I am automatically considered at my second choice, and so on. This strategy maximizes my chances of getting into the best school possible.
reasoning.Student C:
My stated preferences are z > x > w > y. My priority ranks are w: 3, x: 3, y: 4, z: 4. I want to maximize my chances of getting into the best school possible according to my preferences, taking into account the priority ranks.

School z is my top choice, but I have a low priority (4). School x is my second choice, also with a low priority (3). School w is my third choice, with a slightly better priority (3). School y is my last choice, also with a low priority (4).

Since most applicants favor y > x > w > z, it is likely that schools y, x, and w will be highly competitive. School z might be less competitive than x or w, despite being the least favored by most applicants, because my priority at z is low.

Given my preferences and priorities, and the preferences of other applicants, I should stick to my true preferences. Since a rejection never eliminates my chance at schools ranked lower, there is no strategic advantage to misrepresenting my preferences.

Therefore, my ranking remains z > x > w > y.
